meta.title: One Home Chord, Three Ways
meta.summary: Lydian, Ionian and Mixolydian are one home chord at three settings of two dials, and what tells them apart in playing is which single note you lean on.

spans.text: Three settings, one home chord. Put Lydian, Ionian and Mixolydian side by side and the two dials this chapter has been turning — the
— turn out to be the whole story. Lydian raises the first, Mixolydian lowers the second, and Ionian is what both dials look like left alone.

Ionian's empty row is content, not a gap. It has no characteristic note, so there's no second chord that could assert one — what makes it Ionian is precisely that neither dial has been turned, not that something is missing from the table. That reference status is exactly why it was possible to measure Lydian and Mixolydian against it in the first place, note by note and chip by chip.
What separates the three when you're actually playing is one note apiece, not a different set of shapes — the windows underneath are the same five you've always had. Lean on the

props.caption: Both vamps back to back — I–II, then I–bVII, over the same home chord

spans.text: — the same home chord both times, leaning two different directions off it.

One honest caveat before you move on, because this chapter has been careful about it in both directions already. Including a characteristic note in a scale isn't the same as leaning on it in a phrase — actually landing there rather than passing through on the way somewhere else. Making that difference audible on purpose is work for a later chapter; for now, know that the target exists, has a name, and sits at an exact fret whenever you go looking for it.

One more diagram, and it's worth being precise about what it shows. It draws the five windows and their roots, not any mode's notes — that block only knows a quality, major or minor, not a scale, so it can't tell Lydian from Mixolydian apart. That's exactly the point here: the bands and the roots are identical for all three modes in this chapter, because a window is anchored on the root, not on which degree inside it has been raised or lowered. Whichever of the three you're playing, your hand never has to relearn where home is.
